passage:
Monday. In the library's quiet room, Irfan and Hafsa turned a sheet of paper over. "It is next November. We failed. Why?" Irfan wrote: exam weeks, one of us drifting away, customers who never come back. Hafsa added: no clear rule for who decides what. Beside each, they wrote a rule. Exam weeks: orders pause for five days, announced early. Drifting: a monthly honest check-in. No repeat buyers: ask every customer one question after the first order.
Thursday. Exam week arrived. They paused orders, posted a notice, and slept.
Three weeks later, the check-in surfaced that Hafsa was overloaded. They shifted two tasks. Irfan pinned the sheet above his desk.

qa.q: Which day did Irfan and Hafsa write their rules?
qa.a: They wrote their rules on Monday.

qa.q: What is Hafsa feeling at the three-week check-in?
qa.a: Hafsa is likely feeling stressed, since the check-in shows Hafsa was overloaded, which lets the two of them shift tasks.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders add, and why?
qa.a: They could run a tiny paid trial with a few customers, because imagining failure lists risks while a trial shows which ones are real.

qa.q: How might a customer see the notice about paused orders?
qa.a: A customer would see a clear announcement that orders pause in exam week, which shows the team is reliable and protects the customer from surprise delays.

grounding: Shows a pre-mortem on a student venture, imagining failure a year ahead, naming likely causes and attaching a rule to each.

passage: Mehak, you're starting a business in college? Good. Let me tell you what we did, back when I was twenty and ran a cycle-repair service on our campus with two friends, Farhan and Leela. Before we spent a rupee, Farhan made us do something strange. "Imagine it's one year from today and we've shut down. Why?" We sat on the hostel roof and listed it. One: exams, because all three of us would vanish in April. Two: a cofounder leaving. "Saurabh, that's you," Farhan said, "for an internship," and I had to admit it. Three: nobody coming back after the first repair. So we made a rule for each. We'd close in exam weeks and announce it early. Anyone leaving would give a month's notice and train someone. Every customer got a free check-up card for the next visit. We ran for three years, Mehak. We didn't shut down. We graduated.

qa.q: What three reasons for failure did they list?
qa.a: Exams, a cofounder leaving, and nobody coming back after the first repair.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when Farhan named the likely leaver?
qa.a: Saurabh seems a little sheepish but honest, having to admit an internship might pull Saurabh away first.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Making a rule for each imagined failure, like closing in exam weeks and giving check-up cards, because it turned vague fears into plans.

qa.q: How did Farhan see the need for the exercise?
qa.a: Farhan pushed for it before any money was spent, seeing that imagining failure early was the cheapest way to prevent it.

grounding: Shows founders imagining their venture failing after a year, listing exams, a cofounder leaving and no repeat customers, and setting a rule for each.

passage: Ritu and Akash had three evenings before their semester exams, and a pitch to the campus incubator on Monday. Their idea: a late-night snack delivery service for the hostels. Instead of polishing slides, Ritu grabbed a whiteboard in the empty library seminar room. "It's a year from now. We've failed. Why?" Akash groaned, then started. "Exams. We both disappear for three weeks." "A cofounder leaves," Ritu added, looking at him. "You're going on exchange in spring." He nodded slowly. "And nobody orders twice once the novelty wears off." They wrote a rule under each. Exams: pause deliveries and post the dates a month ahead. A cofounder leaving: Akash would write down every supplier contact and train a junior before spring. Repeat orders: a stamp card, every fifth snack free. On Monday the mentor asked, "What could kill this?" They were the only team with an answer ready.

qa.a: A late-night snack delivery service for the hostels.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when Ritu mentioned his exchange?
qa.a: Akash felt awkward and a little guilty but accepting, nodding slowly as he admitted he might be the cofounder who leaves.

qa.q: What else could they add to the pre-mortem?
qa.a: They could add risks like food safety or a supplier raising prices, with a rule for each.

qa.q: How might the incubator mentor see their answer?
qa.a: The mentor would likely be impressed that they had already faced what could kill the idea and made plans, unlike the other teams.

grounding: Illustrates a founding team, short on time before exams, imagining the venture's failure, listing likely causes and setting a rule for each risk.
